questions.question: Explain why the same tectonic force can produce folding in one place and faulting in another. Refer to depth, rate and rock type.
questions.expected_answer: Whether rock bends or breaks depends on its condition, not only on the force. DEPTH and TEMPERATURE: deep in the crust, heat and enormous confining pressure allow rock to deform plastically, so it bends permanently without fracturing; near the surface rock is cold and brittle and snaps. RATE: force applied slowly over millions of years lets rock creep and fold, while sudden force exceeds the rock's strength and fractures it. ROCK TYPE: well-bedded sedimentary strata such as shale and sandstone bend comparatively readily, whereas massive igneous rock such as granite tends to fracture. Rock also passes through a sequence — elastic deformation, then plastic deformation (folding), then fracture and displacement (faulting) — so folding and faulting are stages of one process rather than two unrelated events.

questions.question: Describe, in words alone, a cross-section through a rift valley and a cross-section through a block mountain, and explain how each was formed.
questions.expected_answer: RIFT VALLEY: tension stretched the crust until two roughly parallel normal faults developed. Along each fault the hanging wall slid down, so the central block subsided between them. In cross-section the picture is a wide, flat valley floor with a steep, remarkably straight fault scarp rising on the left and a matching scarp facing it on the right — the two scarps face inward toward each other. The East African Rift is the classic example, with long deep lakes such as Tanganyika and Malawi lying on the floor. BLOCK MOUNTAIN (horst): faulting on both sides of a block left it standing above the surrounding land, either because it was forced up or because the land on either side dropped. In cross-section it shows steep, straight faulted faces on both sides and a level or gently sloping summit, quite unlike the curved crest of a fold mountain. The Ruwenzori Mountains are a horst standing within the East African Rift. Straight edges and steps indicate faulting; curved, wavy crests indicate folding.

questions.question: Account for the landscape of the Cape Fold Mountains and explain how their structure has shaped human activity in the Western Cape.
questions.expected_answer: The rocks are the Cape Supergroup, deposited as sand and mud in a shallow sea and hardened into very resistant quartzitic sandstone. Roughly 250 to 280 million years ago, during the assembly of Gondwana, compression from the south buckled these strata into a series of folds, producing long, narrow, parallel ranges separated by long, narrow valleys, with one set of ranges trending north-south (the Cederberg and the Hex River Mountains) and another trending west-east (the Langeberg, Swartberg and Outeniqua), converging around Ceres and Worcester. Because the folding is ancient and the mountains no longer grow, erosion has had time to work, and in places anticline crests have been stripped away while synclines stand as high ground — inversion of relief. Human activity follows the structure directly: the sheltered valleys have deep soils washed from the ridges and rivers rising in the mountains, so the Hex River Valley grows table grapes, the Breede River Valley wine and the Langkloof deciduous fruit, while the ranges themselves are real barriers, crossed only at passes such as Bain's Kloof, Du Toitskloof and the Swartberg Pass, which is why the region's road network bends around the folds.
